---
title: "Day 3 — The terminal describes the same folders"
---

[Lecture slides](../lectures/03-terminal/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](03-terminal-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)


## Today's question

Can you move around your folders by typing instead of clicking? The computers
that hold large biological data, such as a sequencing facility's server, usually
have no desktop: you log in and type commands. Today you practise those commands
on your own laptop, in a small workspace you create yourself. Tomorrow the same
workspace will hold files from a laboratory exercise.

**Save today:** the `introcomputing-shell` workspace and `navigation-notes.txt` inside it.

## Opening a terminal

Windows students open **Ubuntu**; Mac students open **Terminal**. The
[Windows/Mac setup page](../intro/ubuntu-windows.qmd) shows how. A **shell** is the
program that reads your commands and runs them, and the **terminal** is the window
you type them into. When it is ready, it shows a **prompt**, for example:

```text
anna@laptop:~$
```

Your prompt will look different, and on a Mac it may end in `%`. Never type the
prompt itself: type only the command after it and press Enter.

On Windows, Ubuntu has its own home folder, separate from your Windows Documents
folder. This week we work in that Ubuntu home folder on purpose; the R project
stays in Documents.

## Where am I?

Use `pwd` (print working directory) to find out which folder the terminal is in,
and `ls` (list) to find out what is in it:

```bash
pwd
ls
```

`pwd` prints something like `/home/anna` (Ubuntu) or `/Users/anna` (Mac): your
home folder. `ls` lists its contents, which will differ from your neighbour's.

Now make a workspace for this week and move into it:

```bash
cd
mkdir -p introcomputing-shell/practice
cd introcomputing-shell
pwd
ls
```

`cd` (change directory) on its own takes you home. `mkdir` (make directory)
creates folders; the option `-p` lets it create `introcomputing-shell` and
`practice` in one go, and it does not complain if they already exist. The last
`pwd` should end in `/introcomputing-shell`, and `ls` should show `practice`.

## The same folder in the file manager

To find out whether this is really the same folder you would click through, open
it in the file manager. In Ubuntu on Windows type `explorer.exe .`, and on a Mac
type `open .`. The `.` means "the folder I am in". A window opens showing the
`practice` folder: one folder, two ways of looking at it. Keep the window open.

## Moving between folders

Make two folders for plant data and move down into one and back up again:

```bash
cd practice
mkdir seedlings
mkdir observations
ls
cd seedlings
pwd
cd ..
pwd
```

`ls` shows the two new folders. `..` means the folder one level up, so the two
`pwd` lines end in `/practice/seedlings` and then `/practice`. The workspace now
looks like this, which you can check in the file manager:

```text
introcomputing-shell/
└── practice/
    ├── seedlings/
    └── observations/
```

Now click into `seedlings` in the file manager and run `pwd` in the terminal.
The terminal is still in `practice`: each window keeps its own location.

A command can also take an **option** that changes what it does. Use `ls -l` in
`practice` to find out when each folder was last changed; the folder names are in
the last column. Then use `cd observations` and `ls` to find out what is in the
`observations` folder. `ls` prints nothing at all, because the folder is empty.
Many commands work silently like this; a real problem prints a message.

## When a command fails

Go back to `practice` with `cd ..` and try `cd Observations`, with a capital O.
On Ubuntu this fails, because Ubuntu treats `Observations` and `observations` as
different names. Many Macs accept it. Always type the real spelling, so that your
commands work on every computer.

Then try a folder that does not exist:

```bash
cd no-such-folder
pwd
```

The shell says there is no such file or directory, and `pwd` shows you are still
where you were. A failed `cd` never moves you and never creates anything. When in
doubt, ask "where am I, and what is here?" with `pwd` and `ls`.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: I'm lost. How do I get back to the workspace?

Run `cd ~/introcomputing-shell`, then `pwd`. `~` is short for your home folder,
so this works from anywhere on this computer.
:::

## Names with spaces, and keys that save typing

Inside `practice`, create a folder `day03`, move into it, and create two
folders in it: `readings` and `field notes`. Type the second one with quotes:

```bash
mkdir day03
cd day03
mkdir readings
mkdir "field notes"
ls
```

`ls` shows two folders. Without the quotes, `mkdir field notes` would make two
folders called `field` and `notes`, because the shell splits what you type at
spaces. Quoting works, but names without spaces, such as `field-notes`, are
easier to type.

Four keys make the terminal much less tiring:

- **Tab** completes a name. Type `cd fie` and press Tab: the shell fills in
  `field\ notes/`, where the backslash keeps the space inside the name, just
  as quotes do. Tab only completes names that exist, so it also prevents typos.
- **Up arrow** brings back your previous command. Read it before pressing Enter.
- **Ctrl+C** stops a running command or clears a half-typed one. It does *not*
  copy. To copy and paste in the terminal use Ctrl+Shift+C / Ctrl+Shift+V in
  Ubuntu and Command+C / Command+V on a Mac.

## Two terminal windows

Open a second terminal window and use `pwd` to find out where it starts. Then, in
the first window, `cd` into `readings` and run `pwd` in both windows. The first
ends in `/day03/readings`; the second is still in your home folder. Each shell has
its own current folder, and moving one does not move the other.

Return the first window to the workspace with `cd ~/introcomputing-shell`, and
reach `day03` again with `cd practice/day03`. The first route works from anywhere,
because it starts at your home folder. The second only works from
`introcomputing-shell`: try it from inside `readings` and you get an error.

## A route between neighbouring folders

Inside your workspace, make a small project tree:

```text
route-challenge/
├── inputs/
└── results/
    └── notes/
```

Create it with `mkdir -p route-challenge/inputs route-challenge/results/notes`
and check it with `ls` in each folder.

Use `cd` to find a route from `notes` to its neighbour `inputs`, and check where
you end up with `pwd`. The route is `cd ../../inputs`: up once to `results`, up
again to `route-challenge`, then into `inputs`.

In the file manager, save a plain-text file `navigation-transfer.txt` inside
`route-challenge`. Write down three routes, each with the folder it starts from:
`route-challenge` to `notes`, `notes` to `inputs`, and `inputs` back to
`introcomputing-shell`. Use `..` in at least one and `~` in at least one. Then
open a new terminal window and follow each route from its starting folder. If a
route fails, the starting folder in your note is usually wrong. Correct the note.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answer: the three routes

- From `route-challenge`: `cd results/notes`
- From `notes`: `cd ../../inputs`
- From `inputs`: `cd ..` then `cd ..`, or `cd ~/introcomputing-shell` from anywhere
:::

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## What changes when I run `cd`? What stays unchanged?

Only the terminal's current folder changes. No file or folder moves, and other
windows stay where they were. `pwd` shows the new location.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why can `ls` work without printing any names?

The folder is empty. An error would print a message.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Which of `pwd`, `ls`, `mkdir readings`, `cd readings` creates something?

Only `mkdir readings`. `pwd` and `ls` look, and `cd` moves you.
:::

**Save today:** in `introcomputing-shell`, a plain-text note `navigation-notes.txt`
with the full path printed by `pwd`, the command that brings you back from home,
and three commands with what they do. You can write it in the file manager's
text editor.
